With Agents, the Evals Are the Engineering

The demo works, so you ship. Then a user phrases a question you never imagined and your agent produces confident garbage that nobody catches until the customer does. The thing on the other side of that wall is not a better prompt. It is evaluation, and it is the actual engineering of agents.

Every agent project reaches the same moment. You type a question, the agent reasons through it, calls a couple of tools, and produces an answer that makes everyone in the room nod. Someone says ship it. For a few days, things feel good.

Then someone asks a question you never anticipated, phrased a way you never planned for, and the agent confidently produces nonsense. You change the system prompt to fix a tone problem and somewhere else the agent starts inventing features that do not exist. You want to try the new model everyone is excited about, but you have no way to know whether it will quietly break the three things your agent already did well. That is the wall. Every team building agents hits it, and the practice on the other side is evaluation.

Three things to take away:

  • The testing instincts that made software reliable for decades assume the same input gives the same output. Language models break that assumption on purpose, so unit tests and "I ran it and it looked right" stop working exactly when you need them most.
  • An eval is just a test whose verdict is a graded judgment instead of an exact match. It is how you check quality thousands of times, on every change, without a human reading every output. It is also the only thing that lets you change an agent without fear.
  • Evals are usually sold as a seatbelt. They are actually an accelerator, and over time the suite becomes an asset a competitor cannot copy, because it is built from your failures, on your traffic.

Your old testing instincts stop working

For decades, software ran on a comfortable assumption. The same input produces the same output. Pass two and three to your add function, get five, every time, forever. Unit tests work because behavior is deterministic. Continuous integration works because a passing test today means a passing test tomorrow unless someone changed the code. The whole culture of shipping with confidence rests on that floor.

Build on a language model and the floor moves. Run the same prompt twice and you get two different responses. That is not a bug, it is how the system works, and it is often why it is useful. The non-determinism that lets an agent handle a question you never planned for is the same non-determinism that makes your old tests useless.

The part that takes a while to sink in is that both of those different outputs might be correct. Ask an agent to summarize a quarterly report and there is no single string that counts as the right answer. There are thousands of good summaries and millions of bad ones, and the line between them is not something string matching can express. A unit test asks whether the output equals an exact value. For an agent, that question is close to meaningless. The output will never equal an exact value, and demanding that it does only tells you the model is non-deterministic, which you already knew.

"Looks right" is the failure mode

Without evals, you ship on vibes. You run a few queries by hand, the outputs look right, and that feeling is your release gate. The trouble is that looking right is precisely how these systems fail. A confidently wrong answer looks right. A hallucinated statistic looks right. An agent that researched the wrong company entirely can produce a beautifully formatted report that looks completely right until you check the one number that gives it away.

Picture an agent asked to write a financial report on a car company. The research step misreads the request and pulls information about a long-dead inventor who happened to share the name. The writing step takes that research and produces a polished investment case built on biographical trivia about a man who died a century ago. It gets forwarded up the chain. Nobody notices, because the agent did all of it autonomously and the output is fluent, confident, and formatted correctly. That is a cascading failure, and no amount of eyeballing the final report will ever catch it. The failure happened three steps upstream, where nobody was looking.

This is why agents make the problem harder than a single model call. One call has one place to go wrong. An agent chaining tools has four ways to fail per tool, pick the wrong tool, pass the wrong parameters, misread what came back, do the wrong thing with it, and each step depends on the last. An early misstep does not stay contained. It propagates, invisible at the point it happened, visible only at the end, by which time the cause is buried.

Evals are speed, not a seatbelt

Here is where the argument flips from defensive to offensive. Evals get sold as a way to avoid disaster, a cost of doing business. That framing undersells them badly. A strong test suite does not make a codebase fast because it prevents bugs. It makes the codebase fast because it gives you permission to change things aggressively. You can rip out a module and rewrite it, because if you broke something the suite tells you in seconds. Confidence is what lets a team move.

Evals do exactly this for agents. With a suite in place, you can rewrite your system prompt on a hunch and know within minutes whether you made it better or worse. You can try a new model the day it launches and get a quantified answer about whether it is safe to adopt. The difference between a team that fears every change and a team that ships improvements daily is not talent. It is whether the change comes back with a number attached. A change with a number is a decision. A change without one is a gamble.

There is a compounding benefit hiding in here. Every failure you find in production can become a permanent test case. The agent fails on some strange input, you add that case to your eval set, and now that specific failure can never silently return. Over time the suite accumulates the encoded judgment of everyone who has ever looked hard at your agent. It becomes a record of every way the thing can go wrong and a guarantee it will not go wrong that way again without you knowing. That record is genuinely hard for a competitor to copy, because they do not have your production traffic and they have not seen your failures. The eval suite stops being overhead and becomes an asset nobody else can replicate.

What you actually measure

The instinct to build one giant eval that checks everything is strong and wrong. A grader that tests accuracy, tone, format, safety, and cost all at once is impossible to calibrate, and when it fails you cannot tell which dimension failed. Split it into one concern per check.

One distinction is worth internalizing. A capability eval is a hill you are climbing, something the agent is currently bad at, where you iterate until it passes. The moment it passes, you promote it to a regression eval, a permanent fixture whose only job is to make sure the agent never loses a skill it once had. The life of a healthy suite is a steady conversion of capability evals into regression evals, climbing one new hill while protecting every hill you already climbed.

And one warning that cuts across all of it. Do not write evals that dictate how the agent works. It is tempting to assert that it must call tool A, then tool B, then make decision C. Resist it. A smarter model will often solve in three steps what used to take six, and if your eval checks the path instead of the destination, every improvement breaks your tests for no reason. Grade what the agent produced, not the route it took.

The shift from demoing to measuring

The hardest part of this is cultural, not technical. Teams that build agents grow up on the demo. The demo is how you get buy-in, funding, and the feeling of progress. It rewards the impressive single run. It is also the enemy of reliability, because it trains you to optimize for the best case when production is decided by the worst case. A demo shows you one run that worked. Production shows you the thousand runs nobody watched, including the ones where a user asked something stranger or more adversarial than anything you imagined.

You will know a team has made the shift when the question after a change stops being "does it look better" and becomes "what did the score do." You will know an individual has made it when their first instinct on seeing a failure is not to tweak the prompt but to read the trace and ask why. Fifteen minutes spent reading real outputs is worth more than hours of fiddling with wording, because fiddling without reading is just a more elaborate form of guessing.

Everything else you do, the prompt design, the tool selection, the model choice, the orchestration, is a hypothesis that this change will make the agent better. Without evals, your guesses stay guesses, and you find out from your users whether you were right, which is the slowest and most expensive feedback loop there is. With evals, every guess gets tested and the agent improves on a measured gradient instead of a hopeful one. That is the engineering. The prompt is the easy part. The measurement layer underneath is what turns a demo into a system you can change without fear, upgrade without re-testing the world, and trust enough to put your name on.
